article_text:
In recent decades, Gustav Klimt has become one of the most sought-after artists on the international art market, with his paintings achieving record-breaking prices at auction. From the gilded elegance of his celebrated portraits to the richly patterned views of Lake Attersee completed during his summer retreats, Klimt’s oeuvre embodies the decorative brilliance and artistic innovation that defined Viennese Modernism. The rarity and enduring appeal of these works among collectors have made them some of the most valuable examples of early 20th-century art ever offered for sale.

The market for Klimt reached new heights with landmark sales of such works as Lady with a Fan in 2023, Blooming Meadow in 2025, and Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer in 2025, each reaffirming the extraordinary demand for his masterpieces. Today, some rank among the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, including the 10 paintings discussed below.

Landhaus am Attersee (Country House by the Attersee), 1914 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Landhaus am Attersee (Country House by the Attersee) depicts the forester’s house at the entrance to Austria’s Weißenbach Valley, where Gustav Klimt stayed during his summers on the southern shore of Lake Attersee. In this secluded setting, near members of the Flöge family—including his companion Emilie Flöge—the artist refined his mature approach to landscape painting. With oil on canvas, the artist transformed the humble building and surrounding vegetation into a richly patterned composition of vibrant foliage, vivid color, and mosaic-like brushwork. Unlike his meticulously prepared portraits, Klimt’s landscapes were executed with few preparatory studies, lending them a greater sense of immediacy and spontaneity. Created during the final phase of Klimt’s Attersee period, the work reflects his fascination with nature as a space of visual intensity. Offered at Sotheby’s New York on November 5, 2003, with an estimate of $18–25 million, the painting achieved $29.1 million. The result confirmed the growing appreciation of Klimt’s landscapes, now regarded as some of the artist’s most personal and innovative achievements.

Apple Tree I , 1912 Image Credit: Christie’s. Klimt’s Apple Tree I is a luminous example of his mature landscapes, depicting a single apple tree rising above a dense carpet of flowers and foliage. This oil on canvas is distinguished by its vibrant palette, shimmering brushwork, and richly decorative surface, reflecting Klimt’s interest in nature during his summers at Lake Attersee and the influence of Vincent van Gogh’s expressive approach to color and movement. First exhibited at the Große Kunstausstellung in Dresden in 1912, the work demonstrates Klimt’s ability to turn a simple natural motif into a striking decorative composition. Its provenance includes ownership by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and its restitution to their heirs in 2006. Offered at Christie’s New York with an estimate of $15–25 million, Apple Tree I sold for $33 million on November 9 of that same year. The sale underscored the enduring appeal of Klimt’s garden landscapes.

Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II , 1912 Image Credit: Christie’s. Klimt’s Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II is an oil on canvas depicting the eponymous Viennese socialite and salonnière , who was one of Klimt’s most important patrons and the only sitter to whom he devoted two paintings. The first, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907), is now held by the Neue Galerie New York. The second, along with works such as Apple Tree I (see above), belonged to the Bloch-Bauer family collection that was looted by Nazi authorities after the annexation of Austria in 1938. After a prolonged legal battle, these paintings were returned in 2006 to Maria Altmann and the other heirs of Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer in a landmark restitution case. On November 8 of that year, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II was sold at Christie’s New York as part of an Impressionist and Modern Art Evening Sale. The painting achieved $87.9 million, setting a new auction record for Klimt at the time. In 2016 the work was sold privately by its owner, Oprah Winfrey, who had purchased it at Christie’s, to an anonymous Chinese buyer for a reported $150 million, making it one of the most significant private art transactions of the decade.

Birch Forest , 1903 Image Credit: Christie’s. “I get up early in the morning, usually around 6 am, sometimes earlier, sometimes later. If I get up and the weather is fine, I go into the nearby forest. I am painting a small beech grove, mixed with a few conifers,” wrote Klimt in a letter to M. Zimmerman in August 1903. It was during his summers in Litzlberg, on the shores of Lake Attersee, that the artist developed his profound connection with the natural world. In Birch Forest (Buchenwald) , he captured a secluded grove with precision. The elegant silver trunks rise like “columns in a cathedral created by nature.” Their intricate patterns contrast with the deep green foliage, creating a richly textured surface. Landscape occupied a significant place in Klimt’s mature oeuvre, reflecting his search for harmony and visual rhythm. With each tree trunk bearing its own unique markings, the painting shows extreme attention to detail. Acquired by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and confiscated by Nazi forces, Birch Forest was returned to their heirs in 2006 before appearing at Christie’s New York on two occasions. In November 2006, the lot achieved $40.3 million against an estimate of $20−30 million. Returning to the auction house as part of the Paul G. Allen Collection in 2022, it realized $104.6 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time.

Litzlberg am Attersee (Litzlberg on the Attersee), 1914 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Litzlberg am Attersee depicts the shoreline of Lake Attersee, with houses nestled beneath a densely wooded hillside and a narrow stretch of water in the foreground. Recent scholarship suggests the painting was executed in the second half of 1914. Its vibrant palette, flattened perspective, and densely layered brushwork exemplify Klimt’s decorative approach to landscape. The composition is believed to have drawn in part on a postcard photograph of the lake that the artist sent to his nephew in August 1914. Acquired directly from Klimt by Viennese patrons Viktor and Paula Zuckerkandl, the painting later entered the collection of Viktor’s sister, Amalie Redlich, a Jewish collector who was dispossessed following the Nazi annexation of Austria and deported to Łódź in 1941. After decades in the collection of the Museum der Moderne Salzburg, the work was restituted to Redlich’s heir in 2011. Later that year, it sold for $40.4 million at Sotheby’s New York, surpassing its $25–30 million estimate. A portion of the sale proceeds was donated to the Museum der Moderne Salzburg to support an extension named in Redlich’s honor.

Bauerngarten (Flower Garden), 1907 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Klimt’s Bauerngarten (Blumengarten) (Flower Garden), one of the artist’s most celebrated landscapes, presents an informal profusion of poppies, daisies, zinnias, and roses arranged into a riot of color and pattern. This oil on canvas gives a sense of Klimt’s summers at Lake Attersee and of his evolving approach to landscape, rooted in the symbolic ambitions of the Viennese avant-garde. Painted in the garden of the Mayr-Hof, his summer retreat in Litzlberg, the work shows how the natural and decorative worlds converged under his brush. First exhibited at the Kunstschau in Vienna in 1908, the painting attracted attention for its innovative composition and almost mystical treatment of nature. Offered at Sotheby’s London in 2017 with an estimate in excess of $45 million, Bauerngarten sold for approximately $59.3 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time. The sale underscored the rarity of major Klimt landscapes appearing on the market, with many works of this caliber held in museum collections.

Portrait of Fräulein Lieser , 1918 Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons. A young woman clad in a flower-patterned cape sits in a frontal pose against a vivid red background. Her face is rendered with delicate, precise details that contrast with the looser, more expressive brushwork characteristic of Klimt’s late style. The identity of the sitter remains uncertain. Earlier catalogues identified her as Margarethe Constance Lieser (1899−1965), while more recent research has suggested that she may have been either Helene Lieser (1898−1962) or Annie Lieser (1901−1972), daughters of the Viennese patrons Henriette and Justus Lieser. Klimt began working on the portrait in 1917, with the model visiting his studio in Hietzing nine times during April and May of that year. The portrait was unfinished when he died of a stroke on February 6, 1918. The painting was known to scholars only through a black-and-white photograph, and its whereabouts remained uncertain for decades before it was discovered in Austrian private hands. On April 24, 2024, it was auctioned by Vienna’s im Kinsky, Austria’s second-largest auction house, recognized for its expertise in Klimt’s works and its experience handling restitution-related art sales. Portrait of Fräulein Lieser sold for approximately $41 million including fees, setting a record as the highest price ever achieved for an artwork at auction in Austria. The sale was conducted on behalf of the owners at the time and the legal successors of the Liester family, following an agreement based on the 1998 Washington Principles. The work was purchased by Patti Wong & Associates for an anonymous buyer.

Dame mit Fächer (Lady with a Fan), 1917−1918 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Dame mit Fächer is thought to be the last portrait Klimt worked on before his death in 1918; it was still on the easel in his Vienna studio at the time of his passing. The work represents the culmination of the artist’s late portraiture, combining the human presence of the unidentified sitter with the rich patterns and decorative experimentation that defined his last years. Returning to the square format he first employed in Portrait of Sonja Knips (1898), Klimt placed the figure at the center of the composition and surrounded her with motifs drawn from Asian art, including the phoenix and lotus blossoms. The sitter’s elaborate robe also evokes Klimt’s long-standing interest in textiles and fashion, an area closely connected to his companion Emilie Flöge, an influential Viennese fashion designer. At Sotheby’s London in June 2023, Dame mit Fächer carried an estimate of more than £65 million ($80 million) and was backed by a third-party guarantee. The painting was hammered in at $93.5 million, reaching $108.4 million with fees and establishing a new auction record for Klimt. The result surpassed the previous record of $104.6 million held by Birch Forest , highlighting the extraordinary demand for Klimt’s late masterpieces in the international market.

Blumenwiese (Blooming Meadow), 1908 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. In this painting of the meadows surrounding Lake Attersee, Klimt moves away from a traditional landscape format to offer a dazzling carpet of wildflowers—bellflowers buttercups, daisies, cornflowers, clover, and dandelions—that fills the canvas, Here, the horizonless view, square composition, and flattened pictorial space show the influence of late Claude Monet, Japanese art, and emerging Modernist photography. Executed likely in the summer of 1908, Blumenwiese represents a pivotal moment in Klimt’s landscape painting, when he pushed the genre toward greater abstraction. The radical composition was so unconventional that some contemporary critics dismissed Klimt’s style as the work of a “madman.” Its distinguished provenance, including ownership by Austro-Galician painter Broncia Koller-Pinell and her husband, Hugo Koller, further enhances its historical significance. The painting sold at Sotheby’s in 2025 for $86 million (including fees), becoming the second-most expensive Klimt landscape ever auctioned and reaffirming its rarity and enduring appeal among collectors.

Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer , 1914-1916 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914−16) exemplifies Klimt’s mature portrait style, where realism and decoration meet seamlessly. The subject emerges from an elaborate costume that blurs the boundary between figure and background. Completed after nearly three years of revisions, the painting demonstrates Klimt’s meticulous working process and extraordinary feeling for ornamentation. Commissioned by the Lederer family, among Klimt’s most important patrons, the painting is one of only two full-length portraits by the artist remaining in private hands. It survived Nazi confiscation during the Second World War and was restituted in 1948. Its provenance, later including a time in the collection of Leonard A. Lauder, makes it one of Klimt’s most significant surviving mature portraits. Estimated at $150 million, the painting was the centerpiece of Sotheby’s November 2025 sales. After a dramatic 20-minute contest between two telephone bidders, it realized $236.4 million (including fees), eclipsing Klimt’s previous record and becoming the second-most expensive work ever sold at auction, behind Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi .

article_text:
Mentre per le strade continuano le proteste , la Paris Art Week accende ufficialmente i suoi riflettori sul mercato dell’arte. E la major Sotheby’s sceglie una formula decisamente meno convenzionale della classica esposizione: aprire le porte di un appartamento affacciato sui Jardin des Tuileries e trasformarlo in un luogo da abitare, dove Picasso e Warhol convivono con martini ghiacciati, cucina d’autore e conversazioni senza fretta. Si chiama Chez Sotheby’s , è nato dalla collaborazione con _POLIMENO ed è aperto fino al 24 ottobre (ve lo annunciavamo qui) . Più che una mostra, è una dichiarazione di stile: perché il lusso contemporaneo non consiste soltanto nell’avere accesso a opere straordinarie, ma nel sapere creare le condizioni perché qualcosa accada, perchè qualcosa si accenda. Il desiderio di un’opera, nel pieno del suo contesto espositivo.

Quasi 150 milioni di dollari di arte moderna e contemporanea, un ristorante nel cuore dell’appartamento e un indirizzo strategico, a pochi passi da Art Basel Paris: qui il collezionismo abbandona per un momento il cerimoniale della compravendita e torna alla sua dimensione più seducente, quella della vita sociale. L’idea è recuperare una tradizione profondamente europea, quella delle grandi case private in cui l’arte non era soltanto una questione di possesso, ma anche un pretesto per riunire persone, alimentare conversazioni e far circolare idee. Il riferimento corre ai salotti di Marie-Laure de Noailles, Jacqueline de Ribes e Charles de Beistegui, ma anche a indirizzi parigini entrati nella leggenda, come Le Palace e Le Mathis: luoghi diversi, accomunati dalla capacità di diventare epicentri della vita culturale e mondana. È quello spirito che Sotheby’s e _POLIMENO rileggono in chiave contemporanea, immaginando un ambiente in cui la distanza tra arte e quotidianità si accorcia e la scoperta avviene senza la rigidità del rituale espositivo.

Il dato, naturalmente, è di quelli che non passano inosservati. Le opere disponibili per la vendita privata raggiungono un valore complessivo di quasi 150 milioni di dollari e attraversano l’arte moderna, post-bellica e contemporanea, con nomi del calibro di Pablo Picasso, Henri Matisse, Andy Warhol, Gerhard Richter e Francis Bacon, accanto a una presentazione speciale dedicata ad Alexander Calder. È la più importante esposizione di opere in vendita privata mai presentata da Sotheby’s in Europa. Eppure, il punto non è soltanto il valore economico della selezione, ma il modo in cui viene proposta: capolavori inseriti in un contesto domestico, dove possono essere incontrati lontano dall’atmosfera formale della sala d’aste. Anche il bar diventa parte della narrazione, con opere di Joan Miró, Georges Braque e Fernand Léger a fare da sfondo a un cocktail o a una conversazione. Qui l’arte non reclama necessariamente un’attenzione esclusiva: entra nel campo visivo, incuriosisce, invita a fermarsi. E non occorre essere collezionisti navigati per sentirsi parte dell’esperienza. Basta la voglia di guardare, scoprire e lasciarsi sorprendere.

Al centro dell’appartamento, il ristorante progettato da Tarek Shamma traduce questa filosofia in un’esperienza di ospitalità vera e propria. La proposta gastronomica porta la firma di Erika Blu, chef di Atelier Renata, e accosta classici italiani e dessert francesi, in un dialogo tra culture che riflette lo spirito internazionale della settimana parigina. A completare il quadro c’è Colin Field, storico bartender già alla guida dell’Hemingway Bar del Ritz Paris, con una selezione che spazia dai martini serviti ghiacciati allo champagne di alta gamma.

«Arte e cibo hanno la stessa magia: uniscono le persone», racconta Valerio Polimeno , fondatore di _POLIMENO, che ha sviluppato il progetto insieme al team di Sotheby’s. Una dichiarazione che riassume bene l’ambizione di Chez Sotheby’s: non costruire semplicemente una scenografia per opere eccezionali, ma dare forma a un luogo in cui trascorrere del tempo, incontrarsi e scoprire qualcosa di nuovo. Sulla stessa linea David Rothschild, per il quale la grande arte si apprezza al meglio in buona compagnia. Il focus si sposta così dal possesso alla condivisione, dal valore di mercato al valore dell’esperienza. Aperto tutti i giorni dalle 10 alle 18 fino al 24 ottobre, Chez Sotheby’s è gratuito e accessibile senza prenotazione per le visite generali. Si può entrare per scoprire le opere, concedersi un caffè o un cocktail, oppure ritagliarsi una pausa nel calendario fitto della Paris Art Week. Il servizio pranzo, invece, è su prenotazione ed è già al completo.

article_text:
Werken in de openbare ruimte trekken veelal de aandacht met hun imposante schaal. Zoniet ‘De Maagd’ van Michaël Borremans, dat klein en fijnzinnig op de zijkant van een Gentse betonnen constructie prijkt. Laure van den Hout wordt in die stad getroffen door de uitzonderlijke benaderbaarheid van het werk. ‘ De Maagd kijkt, en misschien dat wanneer passanten hun ogen naar haar opslaan, er in die ontmoeting iets transcendents ontstaat, een wederkerige verlichting.’

Het heeft iets bevreemdends om liftdeuren uit te zien komen op een openbaar plein. Een groepje mensen stapt de werkelijkheid in. Zo oogt het. Waar ze vandaan komen weet ik niet.

De reden dat ik überhaupt registreer dat er een lift verborgen zit in de kolos op het Goudenleeuwplein in Gent is omdat hoger op het beton een kunstwerk mijn blik vangt. Het is een klein portret van een vrouw, ze kijkt opzij, uit haar ogen schieten lichtstralen. Enerzijds ijl, anderzijds onmiskenbaar, als strakgespannen draden. Het kleurenpalet van het portret is op haar huid na vergrijsd: het haar is donker, de achtergrond zwart gemêleerd. Haar witte boord steekt er monter bij af. Het fresco krijgt haar levendigheid door hoe het geschilderde spel van licht het gezicht definieert: op haar neusbrug weerkaatst het, evenals op haar rechterooglid, -wenkbrauw, voorhoofd, oor en haar. Dat ze iets zwarts met een wit boord draagt, roept associaties op met het habijt van een non. Maar deze vrouw is onmiskenbaar hedendaags. Haar kraag die van een overhemd, haar zwarte bovenkleed eerder een trui, het haar onbedekt.

Kunst in de openbare ruimte is vaak groot van formaat. Sculpturen die je vanaf een afstand al gewaarwordt. Of, wanneer het muurschilderingen betreft, meestal metershoog en -breed. Zo niet hier. Dit werk meet slechts 60 bij 70 centimeter, en lijkt nog kleiner doordat het zich zo hoog bevindt. Wie niet omhoogkijkt, kan het werk makkelijk missen. Het geheel is bovendien een eigenaardig samenspel: een betonnen gevaarte met lift, fresco én aan de achterzijde een gigantische kerkklok.

Het fresco is een werk van de Vlaamse Michaël Borremans, zelf woonachtig in Gent. Het draagt de titel De Maagd (2014). In de richting van de ferme lichtstralen die uit de ogen van de maagd schieten, bevindt zich iets verderop in de Sint Baafs Kathedraal het Lam Gods van de gebroeders Van Eyck. Het veelluik waarop ik eerder zag hoe de Heilige Geest goddelijke stralen naar aarde zendt. Anders dan het licht uit de ogen van De Maagd , zijn de stralen daar goud. In religieuze schilderkunst – zoals bij iconen of het Lam Gods – symboliseert goud naast heiligheid en rijkdom, vaak een innerlijk licht, een transcendentie, misschien zelfs in staat om de toeschouwer te verlichten.

Wat betekent het dan dat de lichtstralen uit de ogen van deze maagd niet goud, maar wit zijn? Wanneer we ergens naar kijken geven we het aandacht, kennen we het betekenis toe. De Maagd kijkt, en misschien dat wanneer passanten hun ogen naar haar opslaan, er in die ontmoeting iets transcendents ontstaat, een wederkerige verlichting. Zou je de lijnen van de lichtstralen vervolgens doortrekken dan raken ze de grond voordat ze bij de Sint Baafs aankomen. Het ontbreken van goud, de kledij van de maagd en haar plek midden op een stadsplein maken haar benaderbaar voor iedereen.

Twee keer kort na elkaar is een deel van het kunstwerk verdwenen bij een schoonmaakbeurt van de betonnen kolos, die, vanwege het huisvesten van de klok, ook wel een klokkenstoel wordt genoemd. Twee jaar na oplevering poetste een schoonmaakbedrijf de verftoetsen weg die Borremans rechts van het portret had aangebracht. Vegen die het maakproces onderstrepen. ‘Als je schildert, wrijf je je penselen ook uit naast het doek. Die streepjes heb ik er bewust op gelaten, dan zie je dat het werk echt op die betonnen wand is geschilderd’, aldus Borremans. Een jaar later verdween bij weer een schoonmaakbeurt de handtekening van de kunstenaar, die aan de achterzijde van het beton was aangebracht, in het gedeelte waar de klok hangt. De Maagd komt daarmee in een lange traditie te staan van kunstwerken waarvan een integraal onderdeel door schoonmakers werd aangezien als extern vuil en die daardoor een te grondige poetsbeurt kregen – zoals Martin Kippenbergers Wenn’s anfängt durch die Decke zu tropfen (1987) overkwam – of zelfs in het geheel uitgewist werden zoals een ( Untitled ) installatie bestaande uit bierflesjes, peuken en halfvolle koffiebekers van Damien Hirst in 2001. Over benaderbaarheid gesproken.

article_text:
国立国際美術館は1977年、万博記念公園（大阪府吹田市）内の旧万国博美術館を譲り受け開館しました。2004年には中之島に新築移転し、2027年に開館50周年を迎えます。この節目を前に、2026年度はコレクション展を２期に分けて、当館の開館年である1977年にいたるまでの美術の動向とその背景を所蔵品によって振り返ります。

開館以来、当館がもっぱら照準を合わせてきたのは、同時代（＝コンテンポラリー）に生じた、美術のさまざまな営みです。その時々の「いま、ここ」で、美術家たちは何を考え、どんな作品を世に問うてきたのか。彼ら／彼女らの歩みを追い、浮き彫りにしようとする美術館の試みは、結果として、私たちの生きる現代（＝コンテンポラリー）へと眼を向けさせることにもつながるでしょう。

一方、美術館はまた、あらゆる作品を分類し、整理し、そして歴史化していく場所でもあります。もちろん、現代美術も例外ではなく、たとえば開館当初に呼びならわしていた「現代美術」は、いまの、私たちにとってのそれとは趣きを異にするはずです。最新の動向を追いかけるという課題と並行して、美術館はまた、歴史として蓄積された現代美術に対して「再」考や「再」評価を加え続けていかなければなりません。今回のコレクションでは、「ポップ・アート」や「ミニマル・アート」や「コンセプチュアル・アート」といった、1960年代になって隆盛したいくつかの動向にあらためて目を向けたいと思います。すでに半世紀以上の年月を経た、かつての現代美術たちを回顧し、いままさに生起しつつある美術を捉えるための足がかりを探ることが、主たる目的です。

Kim Hong-sun , the Korean director of “Project Wolf Hunting” and Season 3 of British crime drama “ Gangs of London ,” is shooting “The Hit List,” a martial arts revenge actioner set during Korea’s Joseon era, with Jung Woo-sung and “ Squid Game ” star Wi Ha-jun .

“The Hit List” adapts a Kakao webtoon that has drawn more than 120 million views. The story follows Han Myeong-hoe, among the most powerful men of the Joseon era, who climbed to the top through bloodshed. Opposite him is Baek E-hwa, a woman who loses everything to Han and turns her life over to revenge. Han’s right-hand man, Jang Gil-do, is a fearsome warrior in his own right.

Man Arrested on ‘Miami Vice ‘85’ Brooklyn Set After Brandishing a Knife

Jung, whose credits include “12.12: The Day,” “Hunt,” “A Man of Reason” and “The Good, the Bad, the Weird,” plays Han. Wi, known for the “Squid Game” series, plays Grand Prince Suyang, who relies on Han’s support in his bid to take the throne from his young nephew.

Two of Kim’s “Gangs of London” collaborators have followed him to the set. Lars Cox, who has worked on HBO’s “House of the Dragon” and Netflix’s “The Witcher,” is director of photography. Gaffer Kieran Waites, who has worked on Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” and the “Fast & Furious” films, has also joined.

South Korean sales company Finecut unveiled the project. It said the film pairs Korean storytelling with international production know-how, particularly for its big action scenes and period world. “The Hit List” is Finecut’s second project with Kim after “Project Wolf Hunting.”

Kim’s earlier genre work includes “Traffickers” (2012), “The Con Artists” (2014), “The Chase” (2017) and “Metamorphosis” (2019). “Project Wolf Hunting” (2022) bowed in the Midnight section of the Toronto International Film Festival. It then played Sitges, Brussels and other festivals and was distributed in more than 70 countries. Kim later signed with WME, the agency that represents Park Chan-wook and Bong Joon Ho.

Cheum Film, Studio Take, Library Company and B&C Group are producing, and Mascot Company is presenting. Cameras started rolling in October.
